title: The post-1986 extra advance of bird arrival in ex-USSR nature reserves came mostly from the 60-day temperature window, not from migration strategy or wintering-area warmth, 1948-2018
abstract: Question: a campaign publication (sci:beea9c54) found that bird first-arrival dates in ex-USSR nature reserves moved 0.72 days per decade earlier than local warming predicts in 1986-2018. Does migration strategy or wintering-area temperature explain this extra advance, and is it robust to the temperature window? Approach: Chronicles of Nature Calendar v1.0.5 (483 bird series at 58 sites in 1986-2018), GHCN-CAMS temperature, migration classes from GBIF winter records (CC0/CC BY counts), a species-specific wintering-area temperature index, a fixed European placebo index, a 48-window scan with a window choice from first differences, and site-cluster bootstraps. Results: long-distance (-0.68 days per decade) and short-distance migrants (-0.78) had the same residual trend (difference -0.10; 95% CI -0.81 to 0.73). The wintering-area index changed it by less than 0.06. Short-distance arrival followed European spring temperature beyond local temperature (-0.74 days per C), but the fixed European placebo explained this better than each species' wintering range; long-distance migrants showed no such link. The 60-day window warmed only +0.09 C per decade because it includes late-winter days, while the 20 days before arrival warmed +0.51 C per decade. With the best trend-free window (20 days), the bird residual was -0.18 (-0.47 to 0.25), 75% smaller. Plant onset advanced less than predicted (+0.49), so a bird-plant contrast remains (-0.67; -1.17 to -0.15). Conclusion: the extra bird advance mostly comes from the window choice, not from migration strategy. Limitations: the window is chosen from 40 candidates and short windows can include detection effects; GBIF winter records are a coarse guide to wintering areas; only 81 long-distance series.
